sections.title: Cairn MVP spec
sections.summary: This spec turns prd.md into code, sets the format that `cairn plan` writes, and lists what is already built.

sections.title: Format
sections.summary: Defines the key list that starts each spec section and the rules for how PRD sections count as covered.

requirements.text: Each spec section starts with a list of keys, before any prose.
IDs in keys are written in backticks and separated by commas.
A key applies to its section and every section below it.
A PRD section is covered when it, or a section under it, appears in some Implements, Defers or Context key.
A Defers or Context key also covers the sections under the one it names.
"Under" means in the heading tree, not by ID prefix; the top heading does not namespace its children.

artifacts.description: Key listing PRD section IDs; used for curves, rollup, coverage.

artifacts.name: Files
artifacts.description: Key listing paths the section will touch; a trailing / is a dir; used for plan-time gate detection.

artifacts.name: Depends on
artifacts.description: Key listing spec section IDs; used for stack order.

artifacts.name: Defers
artifacts.description: Key listing PRD section IDs left for later; used for coverage; the viewer shows them as deferred.

artifacts.name: Context
artifacts.description: Key listing PRD section IDs that need no code; used for coverage; the viewer shows no badge.

decisions.text: Coverage follows the heading tree, not ID prefix.
decisions.why: The top heading does not namespace its children, so prd.goal sits under prd.cairn-mvp.

decisions.text: Cover v1 only; presence is the one v2 piece already built and it stays.

sections.title: Package layout
sections.summary: Lists the packages, the pure-core rule, and the services the CLI uses for IO with live and test implementations.

requirements.text: Core takes plain values and does no IO.
Only the CLI touches disk, git, the database or a model, through the listed services.
The PRD's Clock service is Effect's own Clock, and tests use TestClock.
Files go through Effect's FileSystem.
Commands use effect/cli.

decisions.text: Leave out @pierre/words.
decisions.why: It renders markdown to HTML strings through WebAssembly for streaming model output, the viewer would need innerHTML for it, and it knows nothing of {#id} headings; it may suit streaming session logs later.

decisions.text: Use @pierre/highlights for fenced code and diffs; leave out Shiki for code blocks.
decisions.why: Synchronous tokens become Foldkit spans without innerHTML; @pierre/diffs uses preferredHighlighter: highlights, sharing the same lexers.

decisions.text: Leave out a SQLite driver such as better-sqlite3.
decisions.why: @effect/sql-sqlite-node runs on node:sqlite, which needs no native build.

decisions.text: Leave out Rete, JointJS, Cytoscape, Drawflow and LiteGraph.
decisions.why: Each owns its scene and graph state, which would put state in two places beside the Foldkit model.

decisions.text: Leave out elkjs for layout; @dagrejs/dagre (MIT) is the choice when layout stops being fixed.
decisions.why: elkjs is EPL-2.0 or GPL-3.0 and 8 MB.

decisions.text: Leave out the AI SDK (ai, @ai-sdk/anthropic, @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai).
decisions.why: It adds a second schema language and a Promise API beside Effect; effect/ai covers both kinds of model.

decisions.text: Leave out Cloudflare AI Gateway as a dependency.
decisions.why: It is a proxy, not a library; baseUrl in config lets a user route through it.

decisions.text: Leave out Workers AI.
decisions.why: Cairn runs on the user's machine, not in a Worker.

decisions.text: Leave out an ORM such as Drizzle or Prisma.
decisions.why: One table needs no query builder, an ORM would declare row types a second time beside Effect Schema, and the same SqlClient runs on a Durable Object or D1 if v2 needs it.

sections.title: Trace
sections.summary: Defines Trace field by field: both documents with their sections, derived tasks with commits and events, section statuses, warnings and judgments, with no positions; the viewer depends only on this schema.

requirements.text: Trace holds version, feature, baseBranch, the PRD and spec as TraceDocuments, tasks in manifest order, a status for every PRD and spec section, warnings and judgments.
A TraceDocument holds the path, the whole markdown and its TraceSections.
A TraceSection holds id, title without the {#id}, level, line, parent, human, summary and its own plus inherited keys; keys are empty in the PRD.
A TraceTask is a ManifestTask with derived status, waiting, the effective gate, TraceCommits and sorted events.
A TraceCommit holds sha, parents, subject, files, the Cairn-Section sections and the Cairn-Session session or null.
A TraceWarning has a kind, a message, and a taskId and sha that may be null.
TraceSection is declared in the contract, not imported from core's Section.
The trace carries no positions; the viewer lays everything out.
judgments is empty until the judging work fills it.
`summary` is the section's summary in spec.json, null in the PRD and for a section the index does not hold; a trace written without it decodes with null.

sections.title: Links
sections.summary: Defines a deep link in the contract package: a list of typed steps (section, passage, task, stack, segment, diff, commit, file, lines, turn, note) and one Effect Schema, LinkFromPath, that converts between a URL path and those steps. Decoding enforces the ordering rules for a well-formed link and reports failures by step and field.

requirements.text: link.ts defines the step schemas and one Schema that turns a path into steps and steps back into a path, and these are the only definition of a link.
The viewer's route reads links through LinkFromPath and `cairn link` writes them through it, so a printed link and a copied link are always the same text.
link.ts imports IDs from ids.ts and trailers.ts and never from index.ts.
index.ts re-exports link.ts.
A stack or segment step names the stack by its root task's ID, not by its number.
A lines step holds a side (new or old) and a start and end that are positive integers with start <= end.
A file step's path is a non-empty string relative to the repo root.
A Quote is 1 to 500 characters, with whitespace runs collapsed to one space and trimmed.
A NoteId matches ^n_[a-z0-9]{6,}$.

Each step is written as path segments in the form the table gives: /section/<id>, /passage/<id>/<quote>, /task/<id>, /stack/<root>, /segment/<root>, /diff/<head>, /commit/<sha>, /file/<path>, /lines/<n|o><start>[-<end>], /turn/<session>/<turn>, /note/<id>.
Every step argument is encoded with encodeURIComponent, so a file path's / becomes %2F.
The link with no steps is written as /.
A trailing / is accepted when a link is read and is never written.
A single-line range is written as n40, not n40-40.
No step name is api, presence or assets, so a link never collides with a server route or a built file.
Decoding enforces that a diff step comes directly after a task step.
Decoding enforces that a file step comes directly after a diff or a commit step, and a lines step comes directly after a file step.
Decoding enforces that after the first diff, commit or turn step, only file, lines and turn steps may follow.
Decoding enforces that a link has at most one diff or commit step and at most one turn step, and that a turn step is last.
Decoding enforces that a note step is last.
LinkFromPath is an Effect Schema from the path string to Link; decoding reads a link and encoding writes one.
Every ID in a link decodes through its own contract schema.

A decoding failure is a LinkError that gives the step's index, the step's name and the field path, for example `step 3 (file): must follow a diff or a commit` or `step 2 (diff).head: expected 40 lowercase hex characters`.
The contract package takes fast-check as a dev dependency, at the version spec.testing.model-based pins.

tests.text: For every well-formed Link, generated from the step schemas with arbitraries that follow the ordering rules, encoding then decoding gives the same steps, and encoding gives the same path each time.
Quotes and file paths containing /, %, spaces, emoji and surrogate pairs come back unchanged after encoding and decoding.
The path for `cairn link prd.code-view t74 --file packages/cli/src/api.ts --line 40` is `/section/prd.code-view/task/t74/diff/<sha>/file/packages%2Fcli%2Fsrc%2Fapi.ts/lines/n40`.
A file step with no diff or commit before it is refused, and the error names the step and the field.
A lines step that does not follow a file step is refused, and the error names the step and the field.
A task step after a commit step is refused, and the error names the step and the field.
`/lines/n42-40` is refused, and the error names the step and the field.
A bad SHA is refused, and the error names the step and the field.
A bad percent-encoding is refused, and the error names the step and the field.

decisions.text: One Schema in link.ts is the only definition of a link, used by both the viewer's route and `cairn link`.
decisions.why: So a printed link and a copied link are always the same text.

decisions.text: A stack is named by its root task, not its number.
decisions.why: Numbers move when the plan changes and a root's ID does not.

decisions.text: A line is a side and a line number rather than a position in one view.
decisions.why: So the same link works in the unified view and in the split view.

decisions.text: Notes are not stored yet; the note step only names a NoteId (see spec.sessions.trace-store).
NoteId follows the pattern of SessionId, and the notes work stores notes under it.

sections.title: Items and statements
sections.summary: Lets PRD and spec list items carry section-style IDs and adds done-when statement IDs (`StatementId`, `ownerOf`), then extends the trace, the commit trailer and the spec index to record items, statements, the tests that prove them and the tasks that trace them, while older files still decode.

requirements.text: A list item's ID follows the same rules as a section ID, so it decodes through `PrdSectionId` or `SpecSectionId`.
Every field that holds a section ID (`Implements`, `Defers`, `Context`, `prdSections`, a link's `section` step) can hold an item ID with no schema change.
Items are planned against only in the PRD.
A spec's list items may carry IDs, and those IDs parse the same way as PRD item IDs.
`ids.ts` adds `StatementId`, a string matching `^prd\.[a-z0-9]+(?:[.-][a-z0-9]+)*#v[1-9][0-9]*$`.
`ownerOf(id)` returns the part of a `StatementId` before `#v`, as a `PrdSectionId` naming a section or a list item.
`TestId` (`${SpecSectionId}#t${number}`) moves from `spec-index.ts` to `ids.ts`.
A `Cairn-Section` commit trailer decodes `PrdSectionId | SpecSectionId`, so a commit can name the item it builds.
`TraceDocument` gains `items` and `statements` arrays, each in document order.
A spec's `TraceDocument.statements` is always empty.
A `TraceItem`'s `text` is the item's own text without its `{#id}`, `section` is the heading it sits under, and `parent` is the item it is nested in, or else that heading.
A `TraceItem`'s `human` is true when its own text or an ancestor has `<!-- human -->`.
A `TraceStatement`'s `text` excludes the `Draft:` prefix, the human tag and the `{#id}`.
`TraceTask` gains `statements: Array<StatementId>`.
`Trace.sections`, the list of statuses, also holds every item that has an ID.
Each entry in the spec index's `tests` gains `proves: Array<StatementId>`.
The spec index gains a top-level `tasks` array, each entry holding a `TaskId` and its statements with their `id`, `draft` flag and `provedBy` test IDs.
A trace or a `spec.json` written before these fields existed still decodes, with the new fields as empty arrays.
The JSON Schema files are generated again to reflect the new fields.

sections.title: Relation kinds
sections.summary: Declares the eight relation kinds (needs, built on, ordered after, builds, names, implements, depends on, proves) in one typed table in `relations.ts`, with their allowed end kinds and where each is recorded. It also adds the `orderedAfter` field to manifest tasks.

requirements.text: `relations.ts` declares all relation kinds in one place.
`relations.ts` imports IDs from `ids.ts`.
`index.ts` re-exports `relations.ts`.

The `relationKinds` table holds the eight rows of the PRD: needs, builtOn, orderedAfter, builds, names, implements, dependsOn and proves. Each row gives a label, the allowed `from` end kinds, the allowed `to` end kinds and where the relation is recorded.
Every relation kind declares a non-empty `from` list and a non-empty `to` list of end kinds.
The `names` and `implements` relation kinds end on `prd` or `item`.
The `proves` relation kind runs from `test` to `statement`.
A `Relation` must not accept an end whose kind is not allowed by its relation kind's declaration in `relationKinds`.
The relation index reads each relation kind through exactly one extractor.
The extractors are typed as `Record<RelationKind, Extractor>`, so a relation kind added to `relations.ts` fails to compile until its extractor exists.
Adding a relation kind requires no change beyond its declaration in `relations.ts` and its extractor.
`manifest.ts` adds an `orderedAfter` field to `ManifestTask`: an array of `{ task: TaskId; reason: string }` entries that records the `ordered after` relation.
A manifest task without the `orderedAfter` field decodes with `orderedAfter` set to `[]`.
The JSON Schema files in `packages/contract/schema/` are regenerated to include the change.

sections.title: Attempts
sections.summary: Extends the contract's `Event` into a union discriminated by `kind` (status, usage, conflict), so that the orchestrator's events record each attempt's harness, token usage, cost, billing route and failure reason. It also adds the derived `Attempt` type that the trace carries.

requirements.text: The orchestrator reports what each attempt cost and how it ended on the events it already writes.
`Event` is a union of `StatusEvent`, `UsageEvent` and `ConflictEvent`, discriminated by `kind`.
An event line with no `kind` decodes as a status event, so every existing event line still decodes.
A status event carries the attempt's `session` on running, done and failed events, and its `harness` and `attempt` kind on running events.
A status event carries `usage`, `cost` and `route` on done and failed events, and a `failure` reason on failed events.
When a running status event has no `attempt` kind, the attempt kind is derived.
A session on a task that is not an attempt, used for review or for a conflict, is recorded as a usage event with its model, reasoning, harness, usage, cost and route.
`cost` is in US dollars and is `null` when it is not known.
When the route is `subscription`, which bills to a CLI's own plan, `cost` is `null`.
`Usage.input` counts every input token, cached ones included. `cachedInput` is the part of input read from cache. `output` includes reasoning tokens.
Token counts are non-negative integers.
A token count the provider did not give is `null`, never `0`.
Derivation folds only status events through the task machine.
Usage events and conflict events never change a task's status.
The derived `Attempt` type lives in the contract, in `attempts.ts`.
`parseEvent` in the JS entry decodes every member of the `Event` union.
`appendEvent` accepts every member of the `Event` union.
The contract's JSON Schema files are regenerated to match the new event types.

sections.title: Usage in the trace
sections.summary: Extends the Trace contract with per-task attempts, a terminal flag and usage (per-session token counts, API-equivalent estimates, billed cost, allowance shares and a private allocation), plus private account-wide allowance data, and says which consumers see the private fields.

requirements.text: The viewer reads cost and attempts from the Trace, as it does for everything else it reads.
Each TraceTask carries its attempts, a terminal flag that is true when the task reached its attempt or cost limit without verifying, and its usage.
A task's apiEstimate is the sum over its sessions of each session's share multiplied by that session's estimate.
A session's share is 1 for the task's own session and an explicit allocation otherwise.
A task's allowance shares cover only attributable consumption.
A session referenced by more than one commit of a task appears only once in that task's sessions.
The Trace carries an account field holding account-wide use and remaining, per allowance.
The trace builder fills the new fields from the attempts, the usage records and their estimates, and the allowance snapshots.
The fields account, allocated (and the fee behind it) and each AllowanceShare are private.
GET /api/trace serves the private fields.
cairn status --json must not include the private fields unless --private is passed.
cairn status --json with --private includes the private fields.
The demo trace and any shared export must not carry any of the private fields.
A trace written before this change decodes, with no attempts and an unknown estimate.

sections.title: List items
sections.summary: Builds `itemsOf`, a pure function that lists every list item outside a fence with its ID, text, line, section, parent and human flag. Also builds `assignItemIds`, which `cairn ids` runs to fill each `{#}` on a list item with an ID made from its heading's ID and the item's first two words.

requirements.text: `itemsOf(markdown, sections)` in `items.ts` must be pure.
`itemsOf` must return every list item outside a fence, using the fence rules `assignSectionIds` already has.
An item starts at a line that matches `^( *)([-*+]|\d+[.)]) +`.
An item's own text runs until its first nested list, the next item at the same indent or less, a heading, or a blank line followed by a line that is not indented.
An item's ID is a trailing ` {#<id>}` at the end of the item's own text.
A trailing ` {#}` at the end of an item's own text asks for an ID, and the item's `asks` is true.
`itemsOf` must not return the items of a `Done when:` list, because they are statements, not items.
An item is `human` when its own text has `<!-- human -->`, or when its section or any item it is nested in is human.
`assignItemIds(markdown, taken)` in `section-ids.ts` must fill each `{#}` on a list item.
`cairn ids` must run `assignItemIds` after it assigns heading IDs.
An assigned item ID is the ID of the heading the item sits under, then `.`, then the first two words of the item's visible text, lowercased and joined by `-`.
Markdown, backticks and punctuation must be stripped from the item's text before its first two words are taken for the ID.
When an assigned item ID clashes with one already taken, `assignItemIds` adds `-2`, `-3` and so on.
`assignItemIds` must never change an item that already has an ID.
`assignItemIds` must never give an ID to an item that has no attribute.
`assignItemIds` must change only lines that end in `{#}`.
`cairn ids --check` must exit 1 when any list item's `{#}` is left unfilled, as it does for a heading with no ID.

sections.title: Item coverage
sections.summary: Makes each PRD item that has an ID a unit of its own: defines when an item is covered, adds the `unmapped-item` lint rule and widens the existing ID rules to cover items, rolls tasks and status up per item, and extends gates, planner prompts and the trace to items.

requirements.text: A PRD item that has an ID is planned, counted and linted on its own.
An item counts as covered when an `Implements`, `Defers` or `Context` key names it.
An item counts as covered when a `Defers` or `Context` key names a heading or item that the item sits under.
An `Implements` key that names the section around an item must not count as covering the item.
The `unmapped-item` lint rule fires as an error when a PRD item with an ID is not covered.
Item and statement IDs count as known IDs for `unknown-section`. A task or key that names a deleted item is an `unknown-section` error.
The `duplicate-id` lint rule fires as an error across headings, items and statements.
The `wrong-prefix` lint rule also applies to items, as an error.
An item's tasks are the tasks whose `specSections` hold a spec section that implements the item, plus the tasks whose `prdSections` name the item.
An item's status follows the rules in `spec.status.section-rollup`.
A heading's tasks include the tasks of every item under it.
`gateOf` treats a task that names a human item, or that builds a spec section implementing a human item, as tagged, with the reason `tag:human`.
The planner's `spec`, `sections` and `tasks` prompts gain a rule: when a section's items have IDs, name the items in `Implements` and `prdSections`, not the section that holds them.
The trace builder fills `items`, and the status of each item, from `itemsOf` and the rollup.
Until `spec.planning.again` exists, `cairn lint` reports as unmapped each item that was given an ID after its section was planned.

sections.title: Planner service
sections.summary: The Planner service makes six model calls (spec, sections, tasks, splitSection, splitTask, index), each decoded through its schema with one retry, checks that every Mermaid block it returns draws, and never decides gates, IDs, branches, order or the stack diagram.

requirements.text: The planner makes five calls, each with a prompt file in packages/cli/prompts/.
spec(prd) returns spec markdown, with this file as its worked example.
tasks(prd, spec) returns TaskDraft[] decoded through the TaskDraft schema.
Model and reasoning in a TaskDraft are proposals that routing can replace.
splitSection(section, reason) returns two or more sections under the same parent with the same Implements.
splitTask(draft, spec, reason) returns two or more TaskDrafts that together cover the draft's spec sections and files.
index(section) returns the prose fields of an IndexedSection.
A failed decode retries once with the error in the prompt, then fails with a PlannerError.
The model never decides gates, IDs, branch names or order.
The live layer uses the LanguageModel from spec.models.
The test layer replays fixtures: this spec.md, the drafts behind manifest.json, this repo's spec.json and scripted splits.
sections(prd, spec, prdSections) returns new spec sections for the given PRD sections, each saying which existing section it goes under.
tasks(prd, spec, specSections, existing) drafts tasks for the given spec sections, and a draft may depend on an existing task by ID.
The spec and sections prompts say when to draw a Mermaid diagram.
A Mermaid block that does not draw is sent back once with the error, then removed with a warning naming the section.
The model never decides the stack diagram.

sections.title: Stack order
sections.summary: stackOf orders drafts by dependency and returns a set of stacks: parentOf puts a task on the latest of its dependencies when they share one chain, and starts it from baseBranch after they land when they do not.

requirements.text: stackOf(feature, drafts, gates) returns the tasks as a set of stacks.
Tasks are topologically sorted by dependency; among tasks whose dependencies are placed, gated ones go first, then planner order.
IDs are t1… in that order, and branches are <feature>/<NN>-<slug>.
dependsOn is the draft's dependencies, as task IDs.
A task with no dependencies has parent null and starts a stack on baseBranch.
A task whose dependencies all lie on one chain takes the latest of them as its parent.
A task whose dependencies lie on different stacks has parent null and starts from baseBranch once every dependency has landed.
A cycle fails with a PlannerError naming the tasks in it.
worktreesOf gives each task the worktree of its parent or a dependency when that worktree's latest task is one it depends on and no other task has taken it next; otherwise a new one.
The first worktree is the repo's own checkout (null); the rest are wt-1, wt-2, ….
Tasks that can run at the same time never share a worktree.

The spec draws this repo's stacks as a Mermaid diagram from manifest.json: stacks numbered in the order of their first task and named for the second part of that task's first spec section, a solid arrow for a parent, a dashed arrow for any other dependency.
The diagram is redrawn whenever the manifest changes; a viewer test fails when the two disagree.
stackOf takes the manifest's existing tasks, returns them as they are, and orders drafts after them with IDs continuing from the highest.

sections.title: `cairn plan`
sections.summary: cairn plan runs two steps with a review after each: it writes the spec and asks before drafting tasks, then drafts, judges, orders and lints the tasks and asks before writing manifest.json. A second run continues from the files on disk.

requirements.text: Assign missing IDs in prd.md.
If spec.md is missing or --respec is passed, generate it with Planner.spec; if it exists, find what planning again adds.
If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set, run the sections checkpoint on what was written; otherwise print "Judging skipped: TYPESAFE_API_KEY is not set." once.
Write spec.md and spec.json, and print each section written with its line and the PRD sections it implements.
With --spec, stop after the spec; otherwise ask "Draft tasks from this spec? [y/N]", and on no leave the spec on disk.
Draft tasks from spec.md as it is on disk.
Compute gates, order the stack with the existing tasks, ask the stack questions, and lint in memory.
Print what judging changed, then the stack with new tasks marked, lint findings and flag or unsure judgments, and ask "Write manifest.json? [y/N]".
Refuse to write if lint has errors.
Judgments never block the write.
Write manifest.json, then spec.md with the stack diagram drawn again, then spec.json and judgments.json.
--yes answers yes to both questions.
--respec is refused when the manifest has a task that is not pending.
A run with nothing to write prints "The plan is up to date." and exits 0.

Each statement is parsed and given an ID, drafts are reviewed with the person, the planner writes a test for each statement, statements are attached to tasks in spec.json and the trace, and they are shown in the agent's brief, cairn status, gates and the viewer.

The planner must write a test that proves each done-when statement.
Done-when statements must be attached to tasks in spec.json and in the trace.
Done-when statements must be shown in the agent's brief, in `cairn status`, at a gate and in the viewer.
The PRD must be the only record of whether a done-when statement is a draft.
Nothing in `.cairn/` may store a done-when statement's draft status separately from the PRD.

sections.title: Statements
sections.summary: Defines how done-when statements are read from PRD markdown (`statementsOf`), given stable owner-scoped IDs (`assignStatementIds`, run by `cairn ids`), and checked by a new `statement-owner` lint error.

requirements.text: `statementsOf(markdown, sections, items)` must be a pure function.
A statement list is the list that follows a line reading exactly `Done when:` outside a fence; blank lines may sit between that line and the list, and a list inside a fence is not a statement list.
A paragraph that only starts with "Done when" is treated as prose and yields no statements.
A statement's owner is the item the `Done when:` line is nested under when that line is indented under an item with an ID; otherwise the owner is the heading the line is in.
A statement is a draft when its text begins with `Draft:` matched at the start of the item's text, case-sensitive and followed by a space.
A statement carrying `<!-- human -->` is marked human.
`assignStatementIds(markdown, statements)` gives each statement with no ID the ID `{#<owner>#v<n>}`, where `n` is one more than the highest number its owner already uses.
`assignStatementIds` must never renumber a statement that already has an ID.
`cairn ids` runs `assignStatementIds` after assigning item IDs.
`cairn ids --check` fails when any statement has no ID.
Lint reports `statement-owner` as an error for a statement whose ID's owner is not the section or item it sits under, such as a statement copied from another section with its ID still on it.

sections.title: Asking the person
sections.summary: Adds a `statements` call to the Planner that drafts "Done when" statements for PRD sections and items that lack them. It also adds pure core functions to insert drafts (`withDrafts`) and settle them (`settle`), and an interactive step in `cairn plan` that asks the person to accept, rewrite, delete or skip each draft before the spec step.

requirements.text: `Planner` gains a seventh call, `statements(prd, targets)`, returning `Array<{ target: PrdSectionId; drafts: Array<string> }>`, where an empty `drafts` means the target describes nothing to build.

The `statements.md` prompt asks for one to three sentences per target. Each sentence says what a person does and what they then see, uses a named example where one helps, and names no file, function or test.
On a first plan, the targets are every PRD section and every PRD item with an ID that has no statement, apart from the level 1 heading.
On planning again, the targets are only the sections in `replanOf(...).uncovered` that have no statement.
`withDrafts(markdown, drafts)` in core is pure and inserts each draft as `- Draft: <text> {#<owner>#v<n>}`.
For a section, `withDrafts` puts the draft list under a new `Done when:` line at the end of the section's own body, before its first child heading.
For an item, `withDrafts` indents the `Done when:` line and its list under the item.
`withDrafts` must not change any existing line of the markdown.
`settle(markdown, id, answer)` is pure.
`settle` with `accept` removes `Draft: ` from the statement.
`settle` with `rewrite(text)` replaces the statement's text with the person's words, confirmed, under the same ID.
`settle` with `delete` removes the statement's line, and also removes the `Done when:` line when its list is left empty.
`settle` with `skip` changes nothing.
In `cairn plan`, `ask-statements.ts` runs after IDs are assigned and before the spec step.
`ask-statements.ts` first drafts statements for the targets and writes `prd.md`.
For every draft in the PRD, in document order, `ask-statements.ts` prints the draft's section title once, then the draft, then `Is this what you meant? [a]ccept, [r]ewrite, [d]elete, [s]kip:`.
A rewrite answer reads the next line of input as the new text, and an empty line counts as a skip.
`ask-statements.ts` writes `prd.md` after each answer, so an interrupted run keeps what was answered.
Runs with `--yes`, runs with `--dry-run`, and runs whose stdin is not a terminal ask nothing and leave every draft as it is.
With `--dry-run`, the drafts are kept in memory only and written nowhere else.
With `--spec`, `cairn plan` still asks about drafts.
At the end of the run, when any draft is left in the PRD, `cairn plan` prints `Warning: planned against <n> draft statement(s). Confirm them in .cairn/prd.md, or run cairn plan again to be asked.`
A confirmed statement is never asked about and never rewritten.

sections.title: Tracing statements
sections.summary: Ties PRD statements to tasks and tests: planner prompts make each test end with `(proves <statement IDs>)`, `Planner.index` keeps only known IDs, a pure `taskStatementsOf` works out which statements each task carries and which tests prove them, and three lint warnings flag draft, unproved and statement-less items.

requirements.text: The `spec` and `sections` prompts say that each test a section names ends with `(proves <statement IDs>)`.
The `spec` and `sections` prompts say that a section writes a test for every statement of the PRD sections and items it implements that is not tagged for a person.
Draft statements are passed to the planner marked as drafts.
`Planner.index` fills each test's `proves`.
When filling `proves`, code keeps only the statement IDs that `statementsOf` knows.
For each statement ID dropped from a test's `proves`, code prints a warning naming the section.
`taskStatementsOf(task, statements, index)` is a pure function.
A task carries the statements whose owner is one of the task's `prdSections`.
A task that names a PRD section does not carry the statements of the items under that section.
A statement's `provedBy` lists the tests, in the task's `specSections`, whose `proves` holds the statement.
`spec.json`'s `tasks`, the trace's `TraceTask.statements` and `TraceStatement.provedBy` are produced by `taskStatementsOf`.
Lint rule `draft-statement` fires when a statement is a draft.
Lint rule `unproved-statement` fires when a statement not tagged for a person is in no test's `proves` in any spec section that implements its owner.
Lint rule `task-without-statement` fires when a task carries no statement.
None of `draft-statement`, `unproved-statement` and `task-without-statement` is an error; they are warnings.
A statement is part of its section's body, so editing a confirmed statement changes the section's hash.
When a confirmed statement is edited, its spec sections and their tasks are reported stale by the rules in `spec.planning.again`, with nothing new needed.

sections.summary: Adds `formatStatements` to `@cairn/contract/js`, which renders a task's done-when statements as a markdown "Done when:" block. The block goes at the top of agent briefs, into `cairn status --task` and `cairn approve` (as a review checklist), and into the viewer's task detail.

requirements.text: `formatStatements(task, trace, { order })` in `@cairn/contract/js` returns a markdown block headed "Done when:" with one bullet per done-when statement of the task.

In the `formatStatements` block, a statement proved by a test ends with "(proved by <test id>)", a draft statement is prefixed "DRAFT, nobody has agreed to this:", and a statement tagged for a person is prefixed "A person judges this:".
With `order: "document"`, `formatStatements` lists the statements in document order.
With `order: "review"`, `formatStatements` lists the statements tagged for a person first.
The orchestrator puts `formatStatements(task, trace, { order: "document" })` at the top of each agent's brief, as an addition to step 4 of `spec.orchestrator-adapter`.
`cairn status --task <id>` prints the task's line, then the task's Done when block.
Before it appends the approval, `cairn approve <id>` prints the Done when block with `order: "review"` as a checklist with `[ ]` boxes.
`cairn approve` must not ask about each statement. Approval stays a single act.
A statement tagged for a person counts as settled once the task carries a human approval event.
The viewer's task detail shows a "Done when" block after its heading block.
In the viewer's Done when block, draft statements carry a `Draft` tag.
While the task is `blocked_on_human`, the viewer's Done when block is a checklist with the human-tagged statements first.
After the task is approved, the viewer shows its human-tagged statements as settled.

sections.title: Conflict scores
sections.summary: Builds the pairwise conflict score for tasks that can run in parallel: it reads co-change history from git, then scores each pair from shared, coupled, additive and generated files, weighted by churn, into a value in [0, 1) with reasons. It also adds the `conflicts` config block that holds the patterns, threshold, history depth and hotspot limit.

requirements.text: The config key `conflicts.generated` must default to ["pnpm-lock.yaml", "**/demo-trace.json", "packages/contract/schema/**"].
The config key `conflicts.additive` must default to ["**/index.ts"].
The config key `conflicts.high`, the score threshold for a high pair, must default to 0.5.
The config key `conflicts.history`, the number of commits of history to read, must default to 500.
The config key `conflicts.hotspot`, the number of parallel tasks sharing one file before judging asks about it, must default to 3.
`Git.history(n)` must read `git log -n <n> --name-only --format=%H` on `baseBranch`.
`historyOf(commits)` must be pure and return each file's change count and each file pair's co-change count.
`historyOf` must leave out commits that touch more than 20 files.
`scoreOf(a, b, files, history, config)` must be pure.
`scoreOf` must only score two tasks that can run at the same time, meaning neither needs the other directly or through other tasks according to the relation index.
`scoreOf` must return `{ score, reasons }`, where each reason is `{ file, other?, kind, weight }`.
A `shared` reason with weight 0.5 × churn must be produced when both tasks change a file, or when one task declares a directory that contains a file the other changes.
A `coupled` reason with weight 0.25 × churn must be produced when each task changes one of two files that co-change in at least 3 commits and in at least half of the rarer file's commits.
An `additive` reason with weight 0.1 must be produced when both tasks change a file matching `conflicts.additive`.
A `generated` reason with weight 0 must be produced when both tasks change a file matching `conflicts.generated`.
`churn` must be computed as `1 + min(1, changes / 50)`, so a file that changes often weighs up to twice as much.
The score must be `1 − Π(1 − min(0.95, weight))` over the reasons, so it lies in [0, 1) and rises with every shared file.
The `conflicts.generated` and `conflicts.additive` patterns must match paths the same way gate patterns do.
At plan time, `files` must be each task's declared `files`.
Once a task is running, the changed files of its commits and its worktree must replace its declared files in scoring.
Scoring must not use the file an agent is currently in (taken from presence); it scores on diffs alone.

Adding a shared file to a pair never lowers its score.

sections.title: Conflict ordering
sections.summary: Builds `orderingsOf`, which takes high-scoring conflict pairs among new drafts and either stacks the later task on the earlier one through `orderedAfter` or records a recommendation. It also covers the lint rules, the plan output, `undo <n>` and the `splitFile` judgment that go with it.

requirements.text: `orderingsOf(drafts, existing, scores, gates, config)` is a pure function.
`orderingsOf` runs after `stackOf` has ordered the new drafts and returns `{ applied, recommended }`.
`orderingsOf` walks the high conflict pairs, highest score first.
When both tasks of a high pair are new and neither is gated, the later of the two by ID gains `orderedAfter: [{ task: <earlier>, reason }]`.
An ordering is applied only when the later task's needs plus the earlier task lie on one chain, so the later task gets a parent.
An ordering is never applied to a task that is already ordered after another task.

A high pair that involves an existing task or a gated task, or whose later task has needs on other stacks, goes to `recommended` (for example "start t40 before t41" or "build Stack 12 on top of Stack 9").
The manifest is never changed for recommended orderings.
A gated task is never ordered after another task.
No task is ordered after a gated task.
An ordering's reason is the conflict score's reasons written as text, such as `shares packages/core/src/lint.ts (34 changes)`.
`stackOf` computes a task's `parent` from `dependsOn` plus `orderedAfter`.
`dependsOn` still lists only what a task needs. Orderings are not added to it.
The `parent-mismatch` lint rule compares a task's parent with `parentOf` over `dependsOn` and `orderedAfter` together.
A new lint error `bad-ordering` is reported when `orderedAfter` names an unknown task, a task the task already needs, or a gated task, or when a gated task is itself ordered after another task.
Plan output prints a numbered `conflicts` list before the stack. Each line shows the pair, the score, the reasons, and either the applied stacking or the recommendation.
The task review question accepts `undo <n>`, which removes ordering `n`, runs `stackOf` again and prints the stack again.
When `conflicts.hotspot` or more tasks that can run together share one source file, the stack checkpoint asks the `splitFile` question.
`splitFile` is a probability decision. Its input is the file's path, its line count and the tasks' titles, and it asks whether splitting the file would remove more conflicts than reordering the work.
`Judgment.target` gains the variant `{ kind: "file"; path: string }`.
The `splitFile` answer is only reported. Nothing acts on it.

Conflict orderings are recorded in a separate `orderedAfter` field. `dependsOn` keeps listing only what a task needs.
An ordering is applied only when the later task's needs plus the earlier task lie on one chain.

sections.title: Planning a part
sections.summary: Adds `cairn plan <id>...`, which plans only the named PRD headings or list items and everything under them. `partOf` works out the part and `scopeOf` narrows the replan to it. Planner outputs are checked so they stay inside the part, and lint findings for PRD sections outside the part do not block the write.

requirements.text: `cairn plan <id>...` plans one part of the PRD. Each ID is a PRD heading or list item ID, the same text the viewer copies.
With no ID, `cairn plan` behaves as `spec.planning.cairn-plan` describes.
The `cairn plan` command takes zero or more positional ID arguments through `effect/cli`.
Repeated IDs given to `cairn plan` are dropped, and the order the IDs are given in does not change the result.
`partOf(prd, sections, items, ids)` in `part.ts` is pure. It returns either a `Part` or an `UnknownPartIds` listing the IDs it could not find.
`Part.named` holds the IDs given, in document order. `Part.ids` holds the named IDs plus every heading and list item under them.
"Under" means the heading tree plus item nesting from `itemsOf`, as in `spec.format`. An item sits under its heading and under any item it is nested in.
A named list item adds itself and the items nested under it to the part, not the section around it.
Naming the level 1 PRD heading gives the whole PRD as the part.
Part IDs are checked against `prd.md` with missing IDs assigned in memory, so an item whose `{#}` is filled in during this run can be named.
When any given ID is unknown, the command writes nothing (not even IDs), exits 1 and prints one line per unknown ID.

The unknown-ID lines read: `Unknown PRD ID <id>: no heading or list item in .cairn/prd.md has it.` for a missing ID, `<id> is a spec section. cairn plan <id> takes PRD headings and list items.` for a spec ID, and `<id> is a done-when statement. Name its section, <section>.` for a statement ID.
The part ID check runs before `assignSectionIds`, `assignItemIds` and the done-when drafts touch `prd.md`. A refused run leaves every file in `.cairn/` byte for byte unchanged.
`--respec` given with an ID is refused the same way (nothing written, exit 1), with the message `--respec plans the whole spec from nothing and takes no IDs.`
`replanOf` still computes its fields over the whole plan.
`scopeOf(replan, part, index, manifest)` in `replan.ts` is pure and narrows what `cairn plan` acts on in a part run.
In a part run, `uncovered` holds only the uncovered PRD sections and items in `part.ids`, and `Planner.sections` writes spec for them.

In a part run, `rewritable` holds only the sections whose own and inherited `Implements` all lie in `part.ids`. A rewritable section that also implements something outside the part is moved to `staleSections`, so a part run never rewrites spec for another part.
In a part run, `untasked` holds only the spec sections whose `Implements` names an ID in `part.ids`, plus the sections written in this run.
In a part run, the mapping of newly given item IDs (see `spec.planning.again`) is done only for items in `part.ids`.
`staleSections` and `staleTasks` must not be narrowed in a part run. They are reported over the whole plan, as on any run.
When `spec.md` does not exist, a part run must not call `Planner.spec`.
When `spec.md` does not exist, a part run starts the spec with one heading, `# <PRD title> spec {#spec.<prd-title-slug>-spec}`, and `Planner.sections` writes the part's sections into it.
The stack diagram section is added on the first manifest write, as `withStackDiagram` already does.
`Planner.sections` and `Planner.tasks` still get the whole PRD, the whole spec and every existing task, and both calls also get `part.ids`.
In a part run, a new task draft may depend on any task in the manifest, and a new spec section may name any existing spec section in `Depends on`.

Planner outputs in a part run are checked against the part rules. An output that breaks a rule is sent back once with the error, as a failed decode is. If it breaks the rule again, the run fails with a `PlannerError`.
A new or rewritten spec section's `Implements`, `Defers` and `Context` may name only IDs in `part.ids`.
A task draft's `prdSections` may name only IDs in `part.ids`, and its `specSections` may name only sections in the scope.

The `sections` prompt gains a rule for part runs: when the part needs something outside it that is not planned yet, the section says so in its prose with a line starting `Assumes:` that names the outside PRD section in backticks.
A section written in a part run must not plan an assumed outside PRD section or add it to a key.
In a part run, the targets for new done-when drafts are the part's sections and items that have no statement.

In a part run, done-when questions cover only drafts whose owner is in `part.ids`. A draft outside the part, whether left from an earlier run or written by hand, is not asked about and is not changed.
In a part run, the closing warning counts only the part's drafts: `Warning: planned against <n> draft statement(s) in this part.`
In a part run's stack checkpoint, the `complete` question lists only the part's PRD sections, so it does not flag the parts left for later.
In a part run's stack checkpoint, `ordered` and `oneFeature` still see the whole stack.
`lint` runs over the whole plan, and `cairn lint` is not changed: it still reports every PRD section and item that nothing covers.

Before a part run's manifest write, lint findings are sorted into two groups. Blocking holds every error except `unmapped-section` and `unmapped-item` on an ID outside `part.ids`. Any blocking error refuses the write, as step 10 of `spec.planning.cairn-plan` does.
Unmapped findings outside the part are printed after the stack under the heading "Not planned yet", one `file:line rule message` line each, and the manifest write goes ahead.
In a part run, both reviews print a part line such as `part: prd.deep-links (and 4 sections under it)` above what they list.
With `--dry-run` in a part run, the totals line ends with `in part <ids>`.
A part run whose part has nothing to write prints `This part is up to date.` and exits 0, even when other parts are still unplanned.

Over generated heading and item trees, a named item never brings in its section or that section's other items.

`cairn plan prd.b --yes` writes spec sections that implement only `prd.b` and its subsections, writes tasks that name only those sections, and writes the manifest. `cairn lint` then reports `prd.a` as `unmapped-section`.

`cairn plan prd.nope` exits 1 naming `prd.nope`, and leaves `.cairn/` byte for byte unchanged.
`cairn plan spec.x` exits 1 naming `spec.x`, and leaves `.cairn/` byte for byte unchanged.
A draft statement under `prd.a` is not asked about in a `prd.b` run.

decisions.text: A rewritable section that also implements something outside the part is not rewritten but moved to `staleSections`. The section notes this is the author's choice, not something the PRD says.
decisions.why: So that a part run never rewrites spec for another part.

decisions.text: New or rewritten sections in a part run may name only part IDs in `Implements`, `Defers` and `Context`.
decisions.why: Putting an outside section in `Context` or `Defers` would cover it, and the PRD forbids deferring work to make a run smaller.

decisions.text: When `spec.md` does not exist, a part run starts the spec with a single title heading and does not call `Planner.spec`.
decisions.why: Calling `Planner.spec` would write the whole spec.

decisions.text: Outside dependencies that are not planned yet are recorded in prose with an `Assumes:` line, and are not planned or added to a key.
decisions.why: A later `cairn plan` for that PRD section plans it on its own run.

decisions.text: The stack checkpoint's `complete` question lists only the part's PRD sections, while `ordered` and `oneFeature` still see the whole stack.
decisions.why: So it does not flag the parts left for later.

decisions.text: `Planner.sections` and `Planner.tasks` still receive the whole PRD, the whole spec and every existing task, not only the part.
decisions.why: So a new draft can depend on any task in the manifest and a new section can name any existing spec section in `Depends on`.

decisions.text: `staleSections` and `staleTasks` are not narrowed to the part and are reported over the whole plan.
`lint` and `cairn lint` are unchanged and run over the whole plan. In a part run, unmapped findings outside the part are printed as not planned yet and do not block the write.

sections.title: Model catalog
sections.summary: Adds a model catalog and the person's access, harnesses and preferences to routing config, pure catalog functions for eligibility and pricing, and a routing question that recommends a model and reasoning setting per task by expected total cost. Recommendations are recorded on judgments, applied only when the provider is validated, shown in plan output, and can be overridden per task with `set`.

requirements.text: Config's `routing` must hold a `catalog` (version and models), `access` (route, provider, models or "all", optional note), `harnesses` the runner can start, and `prefer` with `subscriptionsFirst`, `ceilingUsd` and `faster`, defaulting to true, undefined and false.
When `routing.catalog.models` is empty, the catalog must be built from `judge.models`, each name becoming an entry with its description, no prices, and access assumed.
Configs written before the catalog existed must route as they did before.
`catalog.ts` must be pure.
`eligibleOf(catalog, access, harnesses)` must return the models the runner can execute: those with some route in `access` for the model's provider and some harness in `harnesses`.
Subscription access must not count as API credit when deciding eligibility.
`priceOf(model, at)` must return the price in effect at `at`, or none; a missing price stays unknown.
The task's `model` decision must classify over the eligible model names only.

The routing question's input must include each eligible model's description, supported reasoning settings and current price or "price unknown"; the task's declared files and their count; whether it is gated; its statements and the tests that prove them; and the person's preferences.
The routing decision's description must ask for the lowest expected total cost of an accepted result within the person's preferences, counting likely retries and repair, not the lowest token price.
When a category has enough history, history must rank the candidates first.

`routeOf` must require that the configured judge provider is validated for automatic routing and that the chosen reasoning setting is one the model supports; otherwise the planner's choice stands and the judgment is `unsure` with the reason.
The thresholds used for routing must be the judge provider's own.
`Judgment` must gain an optional `recommendation` (model, modelId, reasoning, source, applied, evidence, policy, uncertainties, alternative) and an optional `explanation`.
The `explanation` text returned by the provider beside its typed answer must never be parsed.
`Judgments` must gain `provider`, `policy` and `catalogVersion`.
Code must write a judgment's `message` and `evidence` from the provider's typed answer.
`explanation` must be shown under the label "The judge's explanation".

Plan output must list each routed task with its original and routed model and reasoning, the judge and its version, confidence, catalog version, policy and alternative, e.g. `routed t12 sonnet medium → haiku low (judge typesafe jev-1.14.0, confidence 0.91; catalog 2026-11; subscriptions first) · alternative sonnet low`.
The task review question must accept `set <task> <model> [reasoning]`, which overrides the recommendation for that task and prints the stack again.
`set` must refuse a model outside the eligible set, with the reason.

sections.title: OpenAI Decisions
sections.summary: Adds a second DecisionModel Layer that calls the OpenAI Decisions API, with its own config block, thresholds and routing switch, and maps OpenAI's bounded-choice, condition-probability and rubric-score answers onto Judgment answers without changing what each one means.

requirements.text: A second DecisionModel Layer must call the OpenAI Decisions API. It is built with DecisionModel.make over HttpClient.
The request and response shapes in decision-openai.ts must be decoded through schemas written from the OpenAI Decisions guide and its API reference, read on the day the code is written.
No OpenAI request or response shape may be guessed.
Config must have a judge.provider key that is "typesafe" or "openai" and defaults to "typesafe".
judge.automaticRouting is TypeSafe's routing switch and must default to true.
judge.openai.model must be a pinned model name and never "latest".
judge.openai must hold OpenAI's own pass, flag and minConfidence thresholds.
judge.openai.automaticRouting must default to false.
judge.openai.keyEnv must name the environment variable holding the API key and default to OPENAI_API_KEY.
judge.pass, judge.flag and judge.minConfidence must stay as they are and remain TypeSafe's thresholds.
Thresholds must never be copied between providers.
OpenAI judgments must be advisory, with no automatic routing, until a person sets judge.openai.automaticRouting.
An OpenAI bounded-choice answer must map to a RateAnswer with scoreKind "score" that carries the choice's scores.
A bounded choice's scores must never be read as probabilities of success.
An OpenAI condition-probability answer must map to a ProbabilityAnswer.
An OpenAI rubric-score answer must map to a new ScoreAnswer of shape { score, min, max }.
RateAnswer must gain a scoreKind field of "probability" or "score", and TypeSafe's answers must set it to "probability".
verdictOf must scale a score to [0, 1] and then read it against the thresholds of the provider that gave it.
When the provider cannot give the answer type a question needs, the result must be Unanswered with Invalid, so the verdict is unsure and the draft stands.
judgments.json must record the provider and the pinned model for each judgment.
A response with an unexpected shape must produce a JudgeError that names the field.
When OPENAI_API_KEY is missing, judging must skip with a message.

sections.title: Comparing decision providers
sections.summary: Adds `cairn judge --compare --tasks <ids>`, which asks both decision providers the task questions for person-chosen tasks, records each request in a new `evaluations` table in `cairn.db`, and prints per-task answers beside the manifest's assignments plus agreement, latency, token and cost totals. A dollar and request budget limits the run.

requirements.text: `cairn judge --compare --tasks <ids>` asks both providers the task questions for the given tasks. It uses the same `inputsOf` evidence, the same catalog and the same policy, and sets the answers beside the manifest's existing assignments.
The compare command does not choose which tasks to compare. A person picks them and passes them with `--tasks`.
The compare command writes nothing in `.cairn/` except rows in `cairn.db`. The manifest and `judgments.json` are left as they are.

Each provider request is recorded as a row in a new migration's table `evaluations`, with run ID, provider, pinned model version, target, input hash, input, typed answers, the manifest's assignment, latency in ms, reported tokens, cost, and whether the cost came from the estimate or a report.

The command prints one line per task showing the manifest assignment, each provider's answer with its confidence or score, and whether they agree, e.g. `t12  manifest sonnet/medium  typesafe haiku/low (0.91)  openai sonnet/low (score 0.74)  disagree`.
After the per-task lines, the command prints totals: agreement between each pair, latency p50 and p95, tokens and dollars.

Before each request, the command estimates its cost conservatively. Input tokens are the encoded input's characters divided by 3, output tokens are the request's output cap, and both are priced at the judge model's catalog price.
The command stops when the spent total plus the next request's estimate would pass `judge.evaluation.budgetUsd`, or after `judge.evaluation.maxRequests` requests, and prints why it stopped.
The spent total counts the reported cost for a request where there is one, and the estimate otherwise.
If the judge model has no catalog price, the run stops before the first request with `No price for <model> in routing.catalog: the paid comparison cannot start.`
Adding the compare command does not run it. Only a person runs it.
Automatic routing for a provider is turned on only by a person editing config, not by the compare command.

sections.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway
sections.summary: Routes Cairn's API calls (API-sourced planner and the OpenAI Decisions judge) through Cloudflare AI Gateway by default, with a required `gateway` config block covering account, token, billing mode and request logging, explicit `route` keys, secret redaction, and error handling for a gateway that does not serve the Decisions endpoint.

requirements.text: API calls go through Cloudflare AI Gateway unless a person configures otherwise.
Planning that runs on a CLI keeps the CLI's own sign-in rather than going through the gateway.
With `route: "gateway"`, the client's `apiUrl` is `https://gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1/<accountId>/<id>/<provider>`, unless `baseUrl` is set.
`planner.gatewayTokenEnv` falls back to `gateway.tokenEnv` when it is not set.
A config with a gateway route but no `gateway` block and no `baseUrl` fails to decode, with an error naming both `gateway` and `baseUrl`.
With `route: "direct"`, calls go directly to the provider.
Cairn must never choose the direct route on a person's behalf; direct is used only when a person configures it.
A config with `planner.source: "api"` and no `planner.route` fails to decode, with a message that names the field and both values `gateway` and `direct`.
The decode error for a missing `planner.route` in an `api` config written before this change says what to add.
`judge.openai.route` is required in the config.
`gateway.billing` and `gateway.logging` are required fields of the `gateway` block.
With `billing: "provider-key"`, the provider key is sent in the provider's own header, so the provider account is billed and its credits apply.
The docs page states that, for OpenAI under `provider-key` billing, the key has to belong to the project and organization that hold the credits.
With `billing: "byok"`, no provider key is sent and the gateway uses its stored key.
With `billing: "unified"`, no provider key is sent and usage is billed to the Cloudflare balance through Unified Billing.
Under `unified` billing, Cairn prints that this does not use OpenAI credits.
A refusal under one billing mode is reported.
A refusal under one billing mode must never be retried under another billing mode.
`logging` is required whenever a gateway route is used.
Each gateway request sends the per-request logging header Cloudflare documents for the configured `logging` value, using the header name from Cloudflare's docs.
The docs page states that log retention is set in the gateway itself.
The route reported on each attempt is `gateway` or `unified`.
The request body names the configured model unchanged, so the gateway serves the model that was selected.
The TypeSafe judge must not have a gateway route.
`cairn plan` prints `judge: typesafe jev-1.14.0, direct` for the TypeSafe judge.
The gateway token and provider keys are read with `Config.Redacted` and added to the `Redactor`'s secret set.
The gateway token and provider keys must never be written to config, logs or `cairn.db`.

For OpenAI Decisions through the gateway, a `404` or a response that does not decode as a Decisions answer is a `JudgeError` with the message `The gateway did not serve the Decisions endpoint. Set judge.openai.route to "direct" to call OpenAI directly.`
The gateway route for the OpenAI Decisions judge is printed as `experimental` until a person has checked a real response through their gateway.
The test fixture recorded from a person's check of a real gateway response is committed.
The docs must not list the OpenAI Decisions gateway route as supported until the recorded fixture exists.

sections.title: Routing from history
sections.summary: Adds history-based routing: a pure `rankOf` that ranks eligible (model, reasoning, harness) candidates per task category by cost per verified task from recent finished tasks, and wires it into `refine` at the routing checkpoint as a recorded `history` judgment. The judgment can replace the choice when `routing.adaptive` is on, and can send some tasks to the second choice to explore.

requirements.text: `routing.adaptive` defaults to false, and while it is false history only recommends and changes nothing.
`routing.minTasks` defaults to 5.
`routing.window` defaults to 30.
`routing.explore` is the share of ungated tasks sent to the second-choice candidate, and defaults to 0.
`routing.thresholds` defaults to `firstPass: 0.6` and `hours: undefined`.
`rankOf(category, candidates, outcomes, config)` is a pure function.
A routing candidate is an eligible `(model, reasoning, harness)` triple.
A task counts for the candidate triple of its first attempt, and carries the cost of all its attempts, retries and escalations included.
A candidate's history is its last `routing.window` finished tasks in the category, where a finished task is one that verified or failed for good.
A candidate with fewer than `routing.minTasks` finished tasks in the category has no history.
Candidates whose first-pass rate is below `routing.thresholds.firstPass`, or whose median time to completion is above `routing.thresholds.hours`, drop out of the ranking.
The remaining candidates are ranked by cost per verified task, ascending.
Unless `prefer.subscriptionsFirst` is set, a candidate whose tasks all have unknown cost is ranked after the priced candidates, by first-pass rate.
When `prefer.subscriptionsFirst` is set, subscription candidates come first, ranked by API-equivalent cost per verified task where it is known and by first-pass rate otherwise.
`prefer.ceilingUsd` removes candidates whose cost per verified task is above it.
A new model ID has no history, so a new model version starts over.
At the routing checkpoint, `refine` asks `rankOf` before asking the judge.
With history, the top-ranked candidate is the history recommendation, and when the judge chooses differently both choices are recorded and shown.
With no history, the catalog and the judge choose the route, and the plan says `no history in <category>`.
With `routing.adaptive` off, the history recommendation is recorded with `applied: false` and the planner's or the judge's choice stands.
With `routing.adaptive` on, the history recommendation replaces the planner's or the judge's choice.
Turning `routing.adaptive` off again returns routing to the earlier rules.

An ungated task whose ID hashes below `routing.explore`, where the hash is the first 4 bytes of the SHA-256 of the ID divided by 2³², takes the second-ranked candidate, and the plan marks it `exploring`.
The explore choice for a task is the same from one run to the next.
Each history recommendation is recorded as a `Judgment` with question `history`, which is added to the `question` union, and with `recommendation.source: "history"`.

A history `Judgment` carries a `history` object listing each candidate's model, reasoning, harness, task count, cost per verified task, first-pass rate and count of unknown-cost tasks, along with the constraints applied and whether the task was explored.

With `routing.explore: 0` no task ever explores, and a gated task never explores.

decisions.text: A task is attributed to the candidate triple of its first attempt and carries the cost of all its attempts, retries and escalations included.
decisions.why: The first choice is what the router controls.

decisions.text: `routing.adaptive` defaults to false, so history only recommends and the planner's or the judge's choice stands.
Exploration is decided by hashing the task ID with SHA-256 rather than at random.
decisions.why: The hash keeps the choice the same from one run to the next.

decisions.text: History is keyed by model ID, so a new model version starts with no history.
Candidates whose tasks all have unknown cost are ranked after the priced ones by first-pass rate, unless `prefer.subscriptionsFirst` is set.

requirements.text: Add a failed state: running goes there on fail, and start takes it back to running.
The machine's input is the task plus its effective gate.
A gated task reaches done only through approve.
land takes every status but landed to landed: a commit on the base branch is the record that the work is finished, whatever events came before it.

sections.title: Derivation
sections.summary: derive recomputes every task status from manifest, events and commits by folding events through the task machine and landing from git whatever the status, with warnings for anything ignored.

requirements.text: derive(manifest, sections, config, events, commits) recomputes every task from scratch each time.
Group commits by their Cairn-Task trailer; the files they change give each task's effective gate.
Sort the task's events by ts, then by status and actor, so the order of lines in the file never matters.

Fold events through the task machine: running sends start; done sends approve from blocked_on_human when the actor is human, and finish otherwise; blocked_on_human sends finish; failed sends fail; landed sends land.

Send land when the task's commits are reachable from baseBranch, or a commit on baseBranch carries the task's trailer (a squash merge), whatever the task's status. A gated task that lands with no human approval still lands, with a landed-without-approval warning that names the commit.
An orchestrator that reports done for a gated task still leaves it in blocked_on_human; the machine enforces the gate, not the orchestrator.

Anything the machine ignores becomes a warning in the result, not an error: an illegal transition, an approval from a non-human actor, an event or trailer for an unknown task, and a commit on a task branch without trailers.
A pending task with a blocked_on_human task below it is marked waiting, so the viewer can show why it has not started.
This repo's .cairn/events.jsonl starts with one landed line for each task the manifest records as finished, dated by the commit that brought it to main, with a detail naming that commit.

sections.title: Section rollup
sections.summary: A section's status is rolled up from its linked tasks and descendants by an ordered first-match rule list.

requirements.text: A section's status comes from the tasks linked to it or to any section under it.
The first matching rule wins.
Rule 1: deferred or context if a spec key says so.
Rule 2: unmapped if no task links to it.
Rule 3: blocked_on_human, then failed, then running, if any task has that status.
Rule 4: landed if all have landed, done if all are done or landed, pending if all are pending.
Rule 5: in_progress otherwise.
SectionStatus goes in the contract next to TaskStatus.

sections.title: Attempts
sections.summary: Builds the pure `attemptsOf` derivation, which splits each task's status events into ordered attempts with a kind, an outcome and a cost source. It also adds per-task and global attempt and cost limits that make a task terminal, `taskCostOf` for summing a task's cost, and storage of raw usage reports in a new `usage_reports` table.

requirements.text: `attemptsOf(events, catalog, config)` is pure and returns each task's `Attempt`s in order.
An attempt runs from a status event `running` to the next `done` or `failed` event for the same task.
A `running` event with no later `done` or `failed` event for the task is an `open` attempt.
An attempt's `kind` is taken from the event when the event gives it.
When the event gives no kind, `kind` is `first` for the task's first attempt, `retry` when the model and reasoning match the attempt before, and `escalation` when they differ.
A hand-off to a person is a `running` event with a `human:` actor and `attempt: "escalation"`.
An attempt's `outcome` is `verified` when it ends on `done` and `failed` when it ends on `failed`.
On a gated task, a `blocked_on_human` event after `running` ends the attempt with outcome `verified`.
When the event carries a numeric cost, the attempt's cost is that number and its cost source is `reported`.
A `null` cost on an event with route `subscription` stays `null`, with `costSource: "unknown"`.

When the cost is missing but usage is present and the catalog has a price for the model at the attempt's start, the cost is computed and its source is `priced` (see `spec.sessions.api-equivalent-cost`).
Any other cost case has cost source `unknown`.
The `attempts` config has a global `maxAttempts` that defaults to 3, an optional global `maxCostUsd`, and per-task overrides of `maxAttempts` and `maxCostUsd`.
After a failed attempt, a task is terminal when it has reached its attempt limit or when its known cost has reached its cost limit.
`derive` keeps a terminal task in the `failed` state.
A `running` event for a task after it became terminal produces a `past-limit` warning.
`TraceTask.terminal` carries the terminal flag.
The orchestrator must not start a terminal task.
`taskCostOf(task)` sums the cost of every attempt and of every usage event on the task (review and conflict-resolution sessions), and returns how many of those had unknown cost.
`cairn session put --usage <file>` stores the provider's or gateway's usage report as it came, redacted, in the `usage_reports` table.
A new migration adds the `usage_reports` table.
A stored raw usage report must never be reinterpreted. The normalised numbers on the events are kept beside it.

sections.title: Outcome metrics
sections.summary: Defines the pure function `metricsOf`, which groups finished tasks by any combination of category, model, reasoning and harness and computes outcome metrics for each group, such as cost per verified task, first-pass rate, time to done, failure rates and cache use. Tasks with unknown cost are counted in `leftOut` and never treated as free.

requirements.text: `metricsOf(tasks, groupBy)` is pure. Each input task carries its category, attempts, usage events and hold time.
`metricsOf` returns one `Metrics` per group. A group is any combination of category, model, reasoning and harness.
A task belongs to the model, reasoning and harness triple of its first attempt.
Cost per verified task is the known cost of every attempt and usage event of the group's tasks, failed ones included, divided by the number of tasks that verified.
A task that never verified adds its cost to the cost-per-verified numerator and adds nothing to the count of verified tasks.
A task with any attempt of unknown cost is left out of both sums of cost per verified task and is counted in `leftOut`. Unknown cost is never counted as free.
First-pass rate is the share of tasks whose first attempt verified.
Time to completion runs from the task's first `running` to its verified `done`.
Time to completion leaves out time held at a gate (from `blocked_on_human` to the human `done`) and time behind a conflict hold (from a `hold` event to the task's next `running`).
Model failure rates count only `checks` and `agent` failures.
An attempt that failed for `infra` or `upstream` adds its cost to the task and adds nothing to the failure rates.
An attempt that failed for `infra` or `upstream` does not make the next attempt a "first".
Cache utilization is cached input tokens divided by all input tokens.
Reasoning per verified task counts only attempts that reported reasoning tokens.
Tasks with no category are grouped under `uncategorised`.

sections.title: `cairn stats`
sections.summary: Builds the `cairn stats` command, which derives attempts from `events.jsonl` and prints per-category tables of outcome metrics for each model, reasoning level and harness. It also lists routed tasks and, in shadow mode, compares history recommendations with what ran. It has `--category`, `--since` and `--json` flags, and it is read-only and local.

requirements.text: `cairn stats` must derive attempts from `events.jsonl` and print the metrics for the current repo.

`cairn stats` must print one table per category, with one row per combination of model, reasoning level and harness. The columns are tasks, cost/verified, first pass, hours, retry, escalate, terminal, cache and left out.
Every number `cairn stats` prints must show the number of tasks behind it.
A subscription attempt must appear with its tokens but be left out of cost, and its row's 'left out' column must say how many attempts were left out, e.g. '2 attempts (subscription)'.

After the category tables, `cairn stats` must print a 'routed' section. Each routed task gets a line with its task ID, the model change (e.g. 'sonnet → haiku'), the estimated cost, the actual cost and the number of attempts.
The estimate shown for a routed task must be the recommendation's estimated cost per verified task at the time of the recommendation, read from `judgments.json`.
In shadow mode, `cairn stats` must print a section that compares each history recommendation with what ran. Each entry shows the task, both choices and how what ran did.
`--category <name>` must make `cairn stats` print only that one category.
`--since <date>` must make `cairn stats` count only tasks whose first attempt started on or after that date.
`--json` must make `cairn stats` print `{ groups: Array<{ category, model, reasoning, harness, metrics }>, routed, shadow }`.
`cairn stats` must not write anything.
`cairn stats` must not send anything off the machine.

sections.title: Relation index
sections.summary: Builds the relation index in packages/core: a pure `indexOf(source)` that extracts every kind of relation from a manifest, spec index and PRD (or a trace) and answers queries over them, including transitive needs, build order, start-readiness, parallelism and cycle and dangling-end detection.

requirements.text: `indexOf(source)` is pure and reads nothing but its argument.
The `source` passed to `indexOf` is either `{ manifest, specIndex, prd }` or `{ trace }`.
There is one extractor per relation kind, and each turns the source into `Relation`s.
`needs` relations are read from a task's `dependsOn`.
`builtOn` relations are read from a task's `parent`.
`orderedAfter` relations are read from a task's `orderedAfter`.
`builds` relations are read from a task's `specSections`.
`names` relations are read from a task's `prdSections`.
`implements` relations are read from each spec section's own `Implements` line.
`dependsOn` relations are read from each spec section's own `Depends on` line.
`proves` relations are read from each test's `proves`.
The relation index is rebuilt whenever its source changes.
The relation index is never saved.
Callers memoise the relation index on the identity of its source.
`out(id, kind)` returns the relations of that kind from the item to what it points at.
`into(id, kind)` returns the relations of that kind that point at the item.
`needsAll(task)` returns every task the task needs, directly or through other tasks, in build order.
`neededByAll(task)` returns every task that needs the task, directly or through other tasks.
`buildOrder(tasks?)` returns tasks in topological order over `needs`, breaking ties in `TaskIdOrder`.
`canStart(task, statusOf)` is true for a pending, non-terminal task whose every needed task is `done` or `landed` by `statusOf`.
`waitsOn(task, statusOf)` returns the unfinished tasks among those the task directly needs.
`waitedOnBy(task, statusOf)` returns the unfinished tasks that directly need the task.
`canRunTogether(a, b)` is true when neither task needs the other, directly or indirectly.
`dangling` lists every relation with an end that does not exist, and such relations are left out of every other answer of the index.
`cycles` lists the strongly connected sets in the `needs` relation, each set in `TaskIdOrder`.
Tasks in a cycle are left out of `buildOrder` and reported in `cycles`.

sections.title: Section links
sections.summary: Builds `sectionLinksOf`, a pure function that, for a PRD section or an ID'd list item, reports which other sections or items it needs and is needed by through task dependencies, and lists its unfinished tasks in build order, with a transitive mode as well.

requirements.text: `sectionLinksOf(index, prd, id, { transitive })` must be pure.
`sectionLinksOf` must work both for a PRD section and for a list item that has an ID.
A section's own tasks must be the tasks that roll up to it as defined in `spec.sections.item-coverage`: the tasks linked to the section and to every section and item under it.

A link target must be a section or item that one of the needed tasks links to directly, either because the task names it or because the task builds a spec section that implements it, so that the most specific end is named and not every heading above it.
`needs` must hold every target such that one of the section's own tasks needs a task of that target that is not one of the section's own tasks.
Each `needs` entry must carry the task pairs that make the link, in the form `[{ task: "t95", needs: "t94" }]`.
`neededBy` must hold the same links as `needs` in the other direction: targets with tasks outside the section that need one of the section's own tasks, with their pairs.
`next` must list the section's unfinished tasks in `buildOrder`, with tasks that can start first and every other task carrying its `waitsOn`.
A `ready` count must accompany `next`, giving the number of its tasks that can start.
With `transitive`, `needs` and `neededBy` must hold everything before and after the section, in build order, and each entry must name the section through which it is reached.
